guide.title: Unit 2: Poetry I: review guide
guide.intro: Poems compress meaning into a few lines. This unit practices identifying who speaks and who appears in a poem, seeing how a poem's structure and contrasts shape meaning, and explaining the effect of word choice, similes, metaphors, and sound.

sections.title: Speakers and characters
body: The speaker is the voice of the poem, which is not necessarily the poet. Poems can also include characters: people the speaker describes or addresses.
Ask what details reveal about the speaker's or a character's perspective and feelings: what they notice, how they describe it, and what they leave unsaid.
points: A poem addressed to someone (“you”) reveals a relationship.

sections.title: Structure and contrast
body: Structure includes line breaks, stanzas, repetition, and shifts. A shift (often signaled by “but,” “yet,” “now,” or a new stanza) can turn the poem's meaning.
Contrasts, such as past and present, inside and outside, or light and dark, often carry a poem's central tension.
points: Look for where a poem turns.
Compare how the poem begins and ends.

sections.title: Word choice, simile, metaphor, and sound
body: A simile compares using “like” or “as”; a metaphor states or implies that one thing is another. Ask what qualities the comparison transfers.
Diction (word choice) carries connotations: “cottage” and “shack” suggest different things. Alliteration (repeated initial sounds) can link words and set a tone.
points: Explain the effect of a technique, not just its name.
Connotation matters as much as definition.

example.prompt: Explain the metaphor in “My grief is a house with every window shut.”
example.solution: It presents grief as an enclosed space that keeps the speaker in and the world out: grief isolates and darkens, and the speaker hasn't yet opened up to others.

misconceptions: The speaker is a voice the poet creates.
Explain what the device does to meaning.
Line breaks can emphasize words or create pauses and surprise.
Poems can support several interpretations, each needing evidence.

passages.title: Poem 1: “My Father's Hands”
text: (1) My father's hands were rough as bark,
(2) they smelled of oil and cut tobacco;
(3) he fixed the porch light after dark
(4) and cursed the hinges, soft and low.
(5) I never saw those hands at rest,
(6) not once in all the years I knew,
(7) until the morning he was dressed
(8) in someone else's idea of blue.

passages.title: Poem 2: “Two Windows”
text: (1) In winter, from the kitchen window,
(2) the yard is a page no one has written on;
(3) the fence posts stand like pickets of a story
(4) that never got started.
(5) In summer, from the same window,
(6) my children shout across the grass,
(7) the swing creaks out its single note,
(8) and the page is full of their names.

passages.title: Poem 3: “Commute”
text: (1) The train is a long gray thought
(2) that the city thinks every morning,
(3) carrying us, the small ideas,
(4) from one forgetting to the next.
(5) We hold our coffee, hold our phones,
(6) hold on, hold still, hold back,
(7) and at each stop the doors breathe open
(8) and nobody gets off who meant to.

passages.title: Poem 4: “Lesson”
text: (1) My grandmother taught me to fold dumplings
(2) the way her mother taught her:
(3) pinch, pleat, pinch, a crescent moon
(4) of dough in my clumsy palm.
(5) Mine burst in the boiling water.
(6) Hers floated up like small white boats
(7) returning from a long voyage.
(8) She ate my broken ones herself.

questions.prompt: In line 1, the simile “rough as bark” suggests that the father's hands were
choices: always cold
hardened by work and weather
covered in sap from the trees he cut
gentle and soft
questions.explanation: Comparing his hands to bark conveys toughness and texture from labor.
choiceExplanations: The simile concerns texture, not temperature.
It is figurative, not literal.
Bark is rough, not soft.

questions.prompt: Who is the speaker of the poem?
choices: A narrator who never knew the father
A neighbor fixing the porch light
The father himself
The father's child, remembering him
questions.explanation: The speaker says “My father's hands” and refers to “all the years I knew.”
choiceExplanations: The speaker knew him for years.
No neighbor appears.
The father is described, not speaking.

questions.prompt: What contrast is central to the poem?
choices: The father's constant activity in life versus his stillness in death
City versus country
Summer versus winter
The speaker's own youth versus the speaker's old age, many decades later
questions.explanation: Stanza 1 shows busy hands; stanza 2 ends with the first time they were “at rest,” at his funeral.
choiceExplanations: No city and country contrast appears.
Seasons aren't contrasted.
The focus is on the father, not the speaker's age.

questions.prompt: The phrase “someone else's idea of blue” (line 8) most likely suggests that
choices: the father was dressed for burial in clothes that didn't reflect who he was
the speaker chose the father's clothes for the funeral and now regrets choosing the color
the father loved the color blue
the father was cold
questions.explanation: The phrase implies the burial clothes were chosen by others, unlike the oily work clothes the speaker remembers.
choiceExplanations: “Someone else” chose them.
The phrase implies the choice wasn't his.
The line describes clothing, not temperature.

questions.prompt: In line 2, the metaphor of the yard as “a page no one has written on” suggests that in winter the yard is
choices: dangerous
full of activity
empty and quiet, waiting to be filled
covered in printed signs and the marks of other people
questions.explanation: A blank page suggests snow-covered emptiness and absence of life.
choiceExplanations: Nothing suggests danger.
Activity comes in the summer stanza.
The page is figurative.

questions.prompt: How does the poem's two-stanza structure develop its meaning?
choices: It presents the same view in two seasons, contrasting emptiness with a life filled by the speaker's children
It changes setting from the speaker's kitchen to the yard of a neighbor across the fence, comparing two families
It switches speakers between stanzas
It moves from the present to the distant past
questions.explanation: Both stanzas begin “from the (same) kitchen window,” and the contrast lies in what fills the yard.
choiceExplanations: The view is from the same window.
The speaker stays the same.
Both stanzas describe the present cycle of seasons.

questions.prompt: How does the final line return to an image from the first stanza?
choices: The fence posts return as pickets
The blank page is now “full of their names,” completing the earlier metaphor
The kitchen window is replaced by a door
The swing, put away for the winter, is brought back out into the yard by the children
questions.explanation: The page metaphor is extended: winter's blank page becomes summer's written one.
choiceExplanations: The fence posts appear only in stanza 1.
The window is the same.
The swing appears only in stanza 2.

questions.prompt: What does the poem suggest about the speaker's perspective?
choices: The speaker is annoyed by noise
The speaker prefers winter's silence
The speaker is a child watching a parent, wishing for the quiet of winter to return
The speaker finds meaning and fullness in the presence of their children
questions.explanation: The yard becomes a story only when the children fill it with their names and noise.
choiceExplanations: The shouting fills the page with meaning, not annoyance.
Winter is described as an unstarted story.
The speaker refers to “my children.”

questions.prompt: In lines 1–2, the train is compared to
choices: a river
a gray animal running through the streets
a clock
a thought the city thinks
questions.explanation: “The train is a long gray thought / that the city thinks.”
choiceExplanations: No river is mentioned.
No animal is mentioned.
No clock is mentioned.

questions.prompt: The repetition of “hold” in lines 5–6 mainly emphasizes
choices: the passengers' tension and self-restraint
the passengers' eager joy at going to work each day
the speaker's hunger
the speed of the train
questions.explanation: Holding things, holding on, still, and back accumulates into a feeling of constraint.
choiceExplanations: The tone is constrained, not joyful.
Coffee is only one item held.
The repetition concerns the passengers.

questions.prompt: The final line (“nobody gets off who meant to”) most likely suggests that the passengers
choices: are all going to the same place
are lost in a foreign city and cannot work out which stops they need
never reach work
drift through their routines without acting on their intentions
questions.explanation: Read figuratively, the line suggests people continue in habits rather than making the changes they intend.
choiceExplanations: Nothing says they share a destination.
Nothing suggests a foreign city.
The line is figurative rather than about missing stops literally.

questions.prompt: By calling the passengers “the small ideas” (line 3), the speaker presents them as
choices: the speaker's close friends
dangerous rebels
minor parts of a larger, impersonal system
brilliant innovators who are changing the city
questions.explanation: If the train is the city's thought, the passengers are tiny pieces of it, carried along without much control.
choiceExplanations: The passengers aren't described as friends.
Their restraint suggests the opposite of rebellion.
“Small” undercuts any idea of brilliance.

questions.prompt: The poem presents the speaker as
choices: a stranger watching
a grandchild learning a family tradition
the grandmother
a professional cook teaching a cooking class
questions.explanation: The speaker is taught “the way her mother taught her.”
choiceExplanations: The speaker is being taught.
The grandmother is described as “she.”
The speaker's dumplings burst, so they are a beginner.

questions.prompt: The simile in lines 6–7 (“like small white boats / returning from a long voyage”) suggests that the grandmother's dumplings
choices: are poorly shaped
are too heavy to float
are skillfully made and carry a long history
taste of the sea, like boats after a long voyage
questions.explanation: Boats returning from a voyage suggest success and the long journey of a tradition across generations.
choiceExplanations: They float whole, unlike the speaker's.
They float up.
The comparison concerns appearance and history, not taste.

questions.prompt: Which contrast structures the second stanza?
choices: Morning versus night
The speaker's bursting dumplings versus the grandmother's floating ones
Summer versus winter
The grandmother's patient silence versus the speaker's loud shouting in the kitchen
questions.explanation: Line 5 and lines 6–7 set the speaker's failure beside the grandmother's skill.
choiceExplanations: Time of day isn't contrasted.
Seasons aren't mentioned.
Sound isn't contrasted.

questions.prompt: The final line (“She ate my broken ones herself”) most strongly suggests
choices: that the dumplings were wasted
the grandmother's disappointment in the speaker's lack of skill
the grandmother's quiet, protective love for the speaker
that the speaker refused to eat
questions.explanation: Eating the failures herself spares the speaker embarrassment: an act of tenderness.
choiceExplanations: She eats them, so nothing is wasted.
The act is generous, not critical.
Nothing suggests the speaker refused.
